transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05 14:30 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (MedCore Head of ML), Marcus Lee (CTO), Sophie Turner (PM)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
We scoped an initial POC to evaluate open models for clinical note understanding. Agreed on data share, target metrics (p95 latency <250ms for typical 256-token requests, throughput target // 50 RPS peak, accuracy/F1 targets), and a bench plan. Next steps: Redwood to provide shortlist and bench scripts; customer to upload sample data and acceptance criteria.

Topics: success criteria, model shortlist, quantization & cost, multilingual support, benchmark timeline, compliance.

Action Items (auto): see separate action_items field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? I'm Avery, AE at Redwood Infer — sorry Redwood Inference, got the old nick in my head.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Hi, I'm Priya, I run the ML team at MedCore, mainly doing clinical NER and summarization.
[00:18] Marcus Lee: Marcus, CTO. We're sponsoring the POC, looking to see whether open models can get us near production accuracy at lower costs.
[00:26] Sophie Turner: Sophie, Product, will own acceptance criteria and stakeholder comms.
[00:30] Diego Ramos: Diego, SE at Redwood. I'll drive the performance side and help design the bench.
[00:36] Avery Chen: Great. High level: you asked us to help pick a shortlist of open models, size the workload for the POC, and run benchmarks comparing tradeoffs between quality and cost—especially for bilingual English/Spanish clinical notes, right?
[00:48] Priya Desai: Yep. We have a corpus of anonymized clinical encounter notes, about 10k records and we'd like to test NER, structured extraction, and a small summarization task. Multilingual mainly English with ~15% Spanish and a handful of Portuguese. Domain is heavy on medication names, laboratory values, and negation.
[01:05] Diego Ramos: Good to know. A few clarifying Qs: typical request size (tokens)? concurrency/peak RPS expectations? and any strict latency SLO?
[01:14] Marcus Lee: Typical prompt+response is around 180-400 tokens. Peak concurrent users could translate to 30-50 RPS during burst windows. For SLO, we'd like p95 latency under 250ms for single-turn structured extract calls, ideally closer to 200ms if possible.
[01:29] Sophie Turner: For accuracy, Priya's team will propose thresholds but intuitively F1 > 0.88 for key entity classes and hallucination rate < 2% on critical spans would be acceptance.
[01:40] Priya Desai: Yeah those are rough numbers; we'll formalize. Also we need audit logs and retention for 6 months — SOC2-relevant controls.
[01:48] Avery Chen: Perfect. On the model shortlist, we recommended starting with a mix of instruction-tuned and base models to compare quality vs cost. Our initial list: Llama 2-70B-instruct (hosted at lower perf), Mistral-instruct (33B), Falcon-180B-instruct (heavy but good open instr), Mosaic MPT-30B-instruct, and a domain-adapted small model (provisionally called xgen-med) that some partners have tuned. We can also include Llama 3-70B if you want — it's newer; licensing wise we should check.
[02:13] Priya Desai: Are those models good with Spanish? We need multilingual performance.
[02:18] Diego Ramos: Short answer: some are better than others. Mistral and Falcon variants tend to have decent multilingual capabilities when instruction-tuned, but you lose domain adaptation. For clinical lexicon, we expect the domain-adapted xgen-med or a fine-tuned Llama variant to outperform generic models at entity extraction.
[02:34] Marcus Lee: Cost-wise, what's the delta if we run a 70B vs 33B quantized to 4-bit on Redwood Dedicated?
[02:40] Diego Ramos: Ballpark: 70B full FP16 on GPUs will cost several x vs a 33B 4-bit quantized run. With Redwood's batching and KV caching, you can push effective costs down — for POC we typically test both a quantized 4-bit path and an 8-bit path to see quality deltas. We'll include per-1M-token cost estimates in the spreadsheet.
[02:57] Priya Desai: Is there an easy way to determine hallucination rates in our bench?
[03:02] Avery Chen: We'll define a set of gold spans and high-risk queries. The bench will compute false positive extractions and will flag hallucinations. Diego will add a hallucination-check script that compares model outputs to ground truth and also runs adversarial prompts.
[03:14] Sophie Turner: For timeline, how long would the POC baseline and then optimized runs take? We have a go/no-go decision point by end of April.
[03:22] Diego Ramos: Typical POC cadence: week 0 data ingest & baseline config, week 1 baseline runs across 3-4 models, week 2 quantized runs and additional caching/batching configs, week 3 final runs + analysis. That fits a ~3-4 week window. If you need end of April decision, starting immediately is necessary.
[03:37] Marcus Lee: Data ingestion — can we keep it in our VPC? Data privacy is key.
[03:42] Avery Chen: For POC we can do a few options: hosted with customer-provided S3 + presigned access + strict retention, or run on Redwood Dedicated or Private deployment if you want VPC connectivity. For the initial bench, presigned S3 and dedicated capacity is common. We'll also supply audit logs.
[03:58] Priya Desai: We will prefer VPC/Dedicated for the benchmark because of compliance reviewers, but presigned S3 is fine for the initial sample upload.
[04:06] Diego Ramos: Noted. On metrics collection: we'll capture p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost/1M tokens, F1 per entity, precision on critical spans, hallucination percentage, and regression checks vs our baseline model.
[04:18] Priya Desai: Baseline model meaning?
[04:20] Diego Ramos: Whatever you're currently using in production — if none, we'll pick a reasonable open baseline like a 13–30B instruct model. If you already have a provider model, please share sample outputs.
[04:29] Priya Desai: Currently we have a mix of vendor LLM+rules; I'll share the exports.
[04:34] Sophie Turner: For multilingual testing, do we need separate bench runs or can we mixed-batch?
[04:38] Diego Ramos: Best to run stratified tests: English-only, Spanish-only, and mixed. That tells us if quality drops on Spanish or if caching/batching helps mixed throughput.
[04:46] Marcus Lee: Any special hardware requirements? GPUs, inference optimizations?
[04:50] Diego Ramos: We'll use A100-like nodes for large FP16 runs; for quantized 4-bit we can use cheaper GPU types. Redwood runtime will pick kernels automatically, but we should document the hardware mapped to each model run in the bench spreadsheet.
[05:03] Priya Desai: What about tokenization differences across models for clinical abbreviations?
[05:07] Avery Chen: Good call-out. Tokenization and vocab coverage can affect extraction. We'll add a tokenization analysis to the bench (avg tokens per note, tokens for key spans). Some models tokenize 'mg/dL' differently which affects entity boundaries.
[05:19] Sophie Turner: On acceptance thresholds, we said F1 > 0.88. Is that realistic for off-the-shelf models?
[05:24] Diego Ramos: For non-adapted models maybe not; fine-tuning or prompt-engineering/chain-of-thought and retrieval augmentation improve results. We propose three acceptance tiers: baseline (no fine-tune), adapted (prompt + few-shot + retrieval), and tuned (fine-tune or LoRA). We'll show delta per tier.
[05:41] Priya Desai: How do we try retrieval? We have a vector store of clinical snippets.
[05:44] Avery Chen: Redwood supports a retrieval augmentation workflow. For the POC bench we'll simulate retrieval calls (embedding + KNN) and test a few cache/embedding dimensions; Diego will include retrieval latency in the end-to-end.
[05:55] Marcus Lee: Security — we need KMS integration and audit trail.
[05:58] Avery Chen: We support customer KMS for Private/Dedicated; audit logs are available and we'll produce a SOC2 artifacts packet. We'll attach our security brief in the follow-up.
[06:08] Sophie Turner: Back to models: can you rank the shortlist by expected cost/quality tradeoff?
[06:12] Diego Ramos: Rough ranking (quality -> cost): Falcon-180B-instruct (high quality, high cost), Llama3-70B (high qual, mid-high cost), Llama2-70B-instruct (mid-high qual, variable), Mistral-instruct-33B (good quality, mid cost), MPT-30B (mid quality, lower cost), domain xgen-med (if available, best domain quality but depends on tuning). We'll quantify this in the spreadsheet.
[06:36] Priya Desai: For the xgen-med model — is that something Redwood provides or a partner?
[06:40] Avery Chen: It's partner/tuning work — we can either test a partner-tuned artifact or run a LoRA fine-tune as part of POC. We'll note licensing and provenance in the doc.
[06:51] Marcus Lee: If fine-tuning is required, how long and how much data?
[06:54] Diego Ramos: For LoRA-style adaptation, 5–20k labeled examples can move the needle; full fine-tune is heavier. For POC we'll try LoRA/few-shot and see.
[07:04] Priya Desai: On hallucination measurement: how does the bench differentiate hallucinations from partial matches?
[07:08] Diego Ramos: We'll flag outputs that contain entities not present in ground truth and then run a manual review sample for false positives to calibrate thresholds. We'll provide a confusion matrix and an estimated hallucination rate with confidence intervals.
[07:19] Sophie Turner: Any advice on prompt templates for structured extraction?
[07:22] Diego Ramos: Use constrained output formats (JSON schema) and ask the model to refuse when uncertain. Also provide examples (few-shot) and include explicit anchors (e.g., "if not present, return null"). Results are more stable with schema enforcement.
[07:35] Priya Desai: Do you support function-calling style outputs that integrate with our downstream parser?
[07:38] Avery Chen: Yes — Redwood supports function/tool-calling and structured outputs; we can test that path in the bench.
[07:44] Marcus Lee: For cost calc, please show both hosted API and Dedicated reserved capacity options — we want to compare both economic models.
[07:51] Avery Chen: We'll include hosted per-token pricing estimates and Dedicated monthly capacity numbers plus an amortized cost per 1M tokens under expected utilization.
[07:58] Sophie Turner: Who will own the bench runs?
[08:00] Diego Ramos: Redwood will run baseline and quantized tests; MedCore will provide dataset and acceptance criteria; joint review session at end of each week.
[08:08] Priya Desai: Ok. One more: multilingual token labeling — will you score Spanish same as English? We need weighted metrics because Spanish sections are less frequent but higher impact.
[08:18] Diego Ramos: We'll provide per-language metrics and a weighted aggregate where you define weights. We'll also run a separate Spanish-only pass to ensure parity.
[08:27] Marcus Lee: Any red flags on latency with KV cache + streaming for our request sizes?
[08:31] Diego Ramos: KV cache helps for multi-turn; for single-turn structured extraction caching helps less unless many requests share prefixes. Batching and the right sequence length target are bigger levers. We'll test continuous-batching policies in the bench.
[08:44] Sophie Turner: Great. Let's recap and agree on dates.
[08:47] Avery Chen: Recap: Redwood sends shortlist & bench matrix by Friday 2025-03-07; MedCore uploads sample data and acceptance spreadsheet by 2025-03-10; bench baseline week of 2025-03-17; quantized + retrieval week of 2025-03-24; joint review and decision by end-April. Any objections?
[09:04] Priya Desai: Sounds good. I'll coordinate data upload.
[09:07] Marcus Lee: Fine. Please include SOC2 docs in follow-up.
[09:10] Avery Chen: Will do. Diego, anything to add?
[09:13] Diego Ramos: I'll prepare the perf scripts and a sample benchmark runbook. Also I'll include example prompts and the hallucination-check harness.
[09:22] Sophie Turner: Thanks all. We'll await the spreadsheet and schedule the baseline run.
[09:26] Avery Chen: Thanks everyone — meeting adjourned.

Note: transcript occasionally mislabels product names (Redwood Infer, redwood infra) and model tokens; this is expected in auto transcription.
